0.3 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 0.017 grams, supporting a cleaner fat profile. For fruit, fat is usually just a small side note.

11.4 grams of carbs. Glycemic index is 39, helping with steadier carb behaviour. Fibre is 1.4 grams, with only modest fullness and digestion support, so that's a real downside for fruits. For fruit, carbs come down to sugar control and fibre.
0.7 grams of protein. Not enough protein to be a real strength. For fruit, protein is usually too low to matter much.

Vitamin C is 11% daily value, useful for collagen formation and antioxidant support. Vitamin A is only 2% daily value, not bringing much vision or immune support. For fruit, vitamin C and vitamin A matter most.

Potassium is 3% daily value, the best number here but still too low to carry this section. Iron is only 1% daily value, not bringing much oxygen-transport support. For fruit, minerals are usually a bonus.

Pros first: easy fresh-fruit snack. It works with no peeling or cooking, so it is easy to use when the fruit is ripe. Peel adds tart colour. Keeping the skin gives more plum colour, texture, and sharp-sweet contrast. Works fresh or cooked. It can go into yoghurt, oats, salads, compote, sauces, or desserts without much effort.

Cons next: bruises easily. Soft fruit bruises quickly, so quality can drop fast after transport or storage. Ripeness window is short. The best eating window is narrow, and underripe or overripe plums are much less useful. Stone interrupts snacking. The pit makes them less convenient than fully edible bite-size fruit like berries or grapes.

Best bits are easy fresh-fruit snack and peel adds tart colour. Weak spots are low iron and low vitamin A. Best for practical meals and low-calorie volume because it's easy to build meals around and it helps fill out a meal without many calories.
D tier.
